definition.text: A control rule that switches abruptly between two extreme settings, such as fully on and fully off.

facts.text: Most household thermostats are bang–bang controllers: the heater or compressor is either running or not, depending on whether the temperature is above or below the setpoint.
In optimal control, a bang–bang solution is a control that jumps from one bound to the other and never takes an in-between value.
Such solutions appear when the Hamiltonian is linear in the control, so the maximum principle pushes the control to its upper or lower limit.
Bang–bang controls are sometimes truly optimal, but they are also often used simply because they are simple or convenient.

definition.text: An equation from dynamic programming that splits a decision problem over time into a chain of simpler subproblems, following Bellman's principle of optimality.

facts.text: It writes the value of a decision problem at one moment as today's payoff plus the value of the problem left over after today's choice.
Solving it means finding an unknown function, the value function, which gives the best achievable outcome for each state; the matching best action for each state is the policy function.
The name usually refers to discrete-time problems; in continuous time the matching equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman partial differential equation.
It can be solved by backwards induction, by hand in special cases or numerically, but this may be infeasible with many state variables because of the curse of dimensionality.
Economists call dynamic programming a recursive method, because its economic applications usually give a Bellman equation in the form of a difference equation.
It has been used for optimal growth, resource extraction, public finance, asset pricing and many other economic problems.
The first known economic application is credited to Martin Beckmann and Richard Muth; Robert C. Merton's 1973 asset pricing model is a celebrated later one.

title: State and control variables
article: Bellman equation#Analytical concepts in dynamic programming

definition.text: In a decision problem over time, the state is the information about the current situation needed to choose well, and the control variables are what the decision-maker chooses at each moment.

facts.text: Every optimization problem has an objective, such as minimizing cost or maximizing profit, described by a mathematical objective function.
For someone deciding how much to spend over time, wealth is a state variable and how much to consume now is a control variable.
Choosing the controls now may amount to choosing the next state, though other factors usually affect the next state as well.

definition.text: Bellman's rule that an optimal plan has the property that, whatever the starting point and first decision, the remaining decisions must also be optimal from the situation the first decision creates.

facts.text: It tells dynamic programming how to break a decision problem into smaller subproblems.
In computer science, a problem that can be broken apart this way is said to have optimal substructure.
In dynamic game theory, it is analogous to subgame perfect equilibrium.

definition.text: The mathematical study of how the qualitative behaviour of a family of curves or equations, such as the solutions of differential equations, changes as its parameters change.

facts.text: A bifurcation happens when a small smooth change in a parameter causes a sudden qualitative change in how a dynamical system behaves.
Bifurcations occur both in continuous systems described by differential equations and in discrete systems described by maps.
Henri Poincaré introduced the name in 1885.
In ecology, regime shifts linked to a critical or bifurcation point are also called critical transitions.
Systems nearing a bifurcation point show critical slowing down: they recover more and more slowly from disturbances.
Catastrophe theory, which influenced research on regime shifts, is a branch of bifurcation theory.

definition.text: The two main classes of bifurcation: local ones, seen through changes in the stability of equilibria, and global ones, where larger structures of the system collide.

facts.text: A local bifurcation occurs when a parameter change alters the stability of an equilibrium.
Global bifurcations, such as a cycle colliding with an equilibrium, cannot be found just by checking the stability of equilibria.
Saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations are the only generic local bifurcations that truly need just one parameter to be varied.
